text: People ask me all the time, "Dr. Rice,
what do you actually eat? Not what I
tell my patients to eat, not what the
guidelines say, but what are the foods
that I am personally putting on my plate
every single week?" Well, the honest
answer might surprise you. It's not
complicated, it's not restrictive, and a
few of these foods are ones people have
been told to avoid. I'm Dr. Mitch Rice,
a practicing board-certified primary
care physician here in the United
States, and today I'm sharing 10 foods
that I eat every single week and exactly
why each one earns a permanent spot in
my kitchen. The first food that we're
starting off with is a controversial
one, and that is eggs. Eggs are one of
the most complete whole foods that I
know of. They have every single amino
acid your body needs, choline for brain
health and liver function, vitamin D,
vitamin B12, selenium, and bioactive
peptides that support healthy blood
vessel function. And yes, the
cholesterol conversation. The science
has moved significantly on this. For
most people, dietary cholesterol from
eggs has minimal impact on
cardiovascular risk. What matters far
more is blood sugar stability and
inflammation, and eggs actively help
both. A protein-rich breakfast built
around eggs keep blood sugar steady for
hours, which keeps your cardiovascular
system calmer all morning. I eat
anywhere from two to four eggs every
single morning, and I either have them
scrambled or over easy. Now, eggs are my
breakfast anchor. But if eggs truly are
the foundation, the next food that I'm
talking about is where I get the
majority of the rest of my protein. It's
one that probably gets the most pushback
from anything else I'll be sharing on
today's list. Food number two is steak.
I eat steak every single week, and as a
doctor, I do so without any of the
guilt. Here's why. Muscle mass is one of
the most underappreciated pillars of
long-term health. The research on this
is clear. People who maintain lean
muscle mass as they age live longer,
stay metabolically healthier, and have
significantly lower rates of chronic
disease. Here's the chain reaction that
matters. Muscle tissue is your body's
primary glucose storage tank. The more
muscle you have, the more efficiently
your body handles blood sugar after a
meal. Better glucose control means lower
insulin. Lower insulin means less
inflammation, less fat storage, and less
strain on your cardiovascular system,
including your blood pressure. Lean
muscle mass is one of the most direct
tools we have everything running the way
it should as we age, and protein is what
builds and preserves it. Steak is one of
the most complete protein sources
available. It's loaded with creatine,
zinc, B12, and iron, nutrients that
support muscle function, energy
production, and cardiovascular health
simultaneously. Think of muscle mass
like a savings account for your
metabolism. Every gram of protein that
goes towards building or maintaining
muscle is a deposit that pays dividends
in blood sugar control, energy, and
long-term health. The key to steak,
though, is preparation, and how you cook
it does matter. Now, speaking of the
preparation, this is a perfect place to
talk about what I use to cook my steak
every week. Tasty, which is the sponsor
of today's video, has an air fryer that
has become my go-to for me. And the
reason is simple. The built-in smart
dual sensor probe monitors internal temp
in real time and adjusts automatically.
No guesswork and perfect doneness every
single time. I'm also using the new
Tasty grill creates those beautiful
searing marks right inside of the air
fryer itself. It has restaurant crust
with zero mess. And because we're
cooking at 450° Fahrenheit, the cookware
matters. Tasty ceramic coating is
completely PFOA and PFOS free. Clean
cooking at high heat with no
compromises. If you're interested in
trying out one of these Tasty air fryers
for yourself, use my code Dr. Mitch at
the link below. Or if you want to grab
it from Amazon, you can do so using the
other link
If you order during the spring sale, you
get an extra 1-year warranty completely
for free. Now, back to the list. Food
number three is salmon. And this is
something I try to eat twice a week
minimum. Wild-caught salmon is the most
reliable source of EPA and DHA, the
omega-3 fatty acids that directly reduce
inflammation inside artery walls,
improve vessel flexibility, and support
brain health. After age 50, artery
stiffness becomes one of the biggest
drivers of rising blood pressure.
Omega-3s are one of the most studied
tools for slowing that process. I
consider salmon one of the most
important foods on this entire list for
long-term cardiovascular protection.
Food number four is both beans and
lentils. I try to eat some form of beans
or lentils five times a week. They're
the most consistently studied food
across every long-lived population in
the world, and the reason is
straightforward. They deliver potassium,
magnesium, soluble fiber, and protein
all in one package. Potassium relaxes
artery walls, magnesium calms the
nervous system, and fiber feeds the gut
bacteria that reduce cardiovascular
inflammation. Food number five is cooked
tomatoes. Specifically cooked tomatoes
because it releases a compound called
lycopene. Lycopene is the compound that
gives tomatoes their red color and
accumulates directly inside artery walls
to protect LDL from oxidation. This
helps reduce plaque buildup in artery
walls, and in some cases can actually
reverse plaque buildup. This is one of
the least celebrated but most
research-backed cardiovascular foods
available, and it costs almost nothing.
Food number six on this list is
blueberries. I try to eat about two to
three handfuls of blueberries five times
a week. Blueberries are rich in
flavonoids and anthocyanins that improve
the responsiveness of the inner lining
of your arteries. They reduce oxidative
stress in blood vessels, lower
inflammation, and support stable blood
sugar. A large study found that eating
blueberries daily for eight weeks
produced blood pressure reductions
comparable to some medications. Frozen
blueberries work just as well as fresh,
and I try to add them to plain Greek
yogurt or eat them with eggs in the
morning. Food number seven on this list
is chicken. Again, similar to steak,
chicken, especially chicken breasts, are
loaded with protein. Protein is
absolutely essential for muscle mass,
and again, it's one of the most
underappreciated pillars of long-term
health. Remember the savings account
analogy that I talked about before?
Every gram of protein that goes towards
building or maintaining muscle is a
deposit that pays dividends in blood
sugar control, energy, and long-term
health. Chicken is a phenomenal way to
get that protein. Food number eight is
avocado. Avocados are loaded with
potassium. They actually have about two
times the potassium than a banana does
ounce for ounce, along with healthy
monounsaturated fats and some fiber. The
fat in avocado also helps you absorb the
fat-soluble nutrients from everything
else you eat alongside it. It also helps
make the lycopene from tomatoes more
bioavailable. Think of an avocado as the
nutrient amplifier on the plate. I try
to eat half an avocado most days with
eggs or just sliced with a little salt
substitute. Food number nine is plain
Greek yogurt. The reason for this choice
is simple. It's high in protein, it has
probiotics, loads of calcium and
potassium, and unlike most breakfast
carbs, it does not spike blood sugar.
The gut-cardiovascular connection is one
of the most exciting areas of current
research. The bacteria in fermented
dairy produce compounds that reduce
inflammation, improve blood vessel
flexibility, and lower sympathetic
nervous system tone, all of which
support healthier blood pressure over
time. Plain full-fat Greek yogurt is
what I buy, not flavored stuff, not
sweetened, and I add some blueberries
and potentially a little bit of cinnamon
and maple syrup. Food number 10 is
sardines. I know sardines sound a little
bit gross, but hear me out on this one.
Sardines are one of the most
nutrient-dense, affordable foods on the
planet. They're loaded with omega-3s,
calcium, vitamin D, B12, and selenium.
They're lower on the food chain, so they
accumulate with almost no mercury, and
they're shelf-stable, which means
they're always available. I eat them
straight from the can with some olive
oil, a squeeze of lemon, or mixed with
avocado. If salmon is the premium option
for omega-3s, sardines are the everyday
option, and I try to use both. If this
video gave you a practical starting
point for your own weekly eating, please
consider subscribing, as it really does
help push this message out to the people
that need to hear it the most. Finally,
so whether you eat or drink or whatever
you do, do it all for the glory of God.
This is from 1 Corinthians chapter 10,
